transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Acme Head ML Infra), Aisha Khan (Acme Platform Eng), Ben Ross (Acme SRE)

Summary: Deep technical session on Redwood KV cache architecture and troubleshooting. Focus areas: eviction behavior, paging to disk/NVMe, long-context handling, prefix reuse/warmup, interactions with batching and quantization, and practical diagnostics.

Topics: KV cache eviction policies, memory pressure, paging fallbacks, cache sharding, cache warm/rehydration, cache metrics to track, recommended mitigations for tail latency.

[00:00] Jordan: alright folks, thanks for joining. we scheduled 60 minutes to go deep on KV cache internals and troubleshooting. Priya will lead the technical portion. quick intro from everyone?

[00:12] Carlos: yeah hi Carlos here. we run production LLM endpoints for customer support, about 6 models, mixed lengths. we've been seeing tail latency spikes when context gets long and cache misses ramp. looking for root causes and mitigations.

[00:26] Priya: great. high level first - the KV cache in the runtime stores per layer key and value tensors for decoded tokens so that generation is O(1) for repeated tokens. eviction/paging happens when GPU memory is constrained or when we want to free room for other sessions. common policies are LRU with priority tiers and TTL heuristics for streaming sessions.

[00:48] Ben: when you say paging, do you mean to host memory or NVMe? we're seeing GPU memory go above threshold and then lots of memcopy to host which spikes latency.

[00:59] Priya: good question. we have two fallback levels depending on deployment: host RAM paging, and on Dedicated/Private with NVMe backing, we page to local SSD. paging path is asynchronous but still adds 10s-100s ms depending on transfer sizes and PCIe gen. if you see sudden memcopies, likely the runtime is evicting KV pages for other hotter sessions.

[01:20] Carlos: our workload has many long prefix chats where prefix reuse matters - agents reuse a 2k token system prompt accross sessions. how does prefix reuse interact with eviction?

[01:32] Priya: prefix reuse is the biggest win for KV cache. if the prefix is warm in cache and not evicted, subsequent generation only needs to append new tokens. eviction chances depend on cache capacity and policy. for example, LRU will evict least recently used prefixes which can be a problem for long-lived but infrequently updated prefixes. we recommend pinning hot prefixes where feasible or using a separate pinned cache tier for system prompts.

[01:54] Aisha: how do we pin? is that a runtime flag or a config in the model routing?

[01:59] Priya: config. in Dedicated and Private we expose a pinning config per route. pinned entries don't get evicted except under critical memory pressure; they may be compressed or quantized to save space. in hosted setup we can request pinning for enterprise customers and set higher priority.

[02:14] Jordan: quick note - we can also recommend a model variant with a smaller KV footprint if prefix reuse is low, or apply 4-bit quantization on KV tensors to reduce memory. more on that soon.

[02:25] Ben: quantizing KV tensors sounds risky for quality. any evidence?

[02:29] Priya: we do tiered quantization experiments. quantizing KV caches to 8-bit or 4-bit often has minimal impact on generation for most decoder models when done with bias correction and layer-wise scaling. quality delta is workload dependent; we run evals on your prompts to confirm. quantization reduces memory and reduces eviction/paging events.

[02:50] Carlos: okay, what metrics should we look at in our telemetry to identify cache-related tail latency?

[02:56] Priya: key metrics: cache.hit_rate (overall and per route), cache.evictions.count, cache.pages_out.count, cache.pages_in.latency P50/P95, gpu.memory.used, gpu.memcopy.host_ms, model.request.latency.p95, batch_size distributions, and queued_batches. also trace token-emit timings to see where the spike happens - often the ms gap aligns with a page-in.

[03:25] Aisha: we can extract those. what about sharded GPU clusters? we shard KV cache across GPUs; if one GPU is hot and others idle, could that cause imbalance?

[03:34] Priya: yes. we shard per-layer KV tensors across available accelerators. imbalance happens when request distribution is skewed by session affinity or routing rules. our runtime supports rebalancing and cross-GPU eviction policies, but rebalancing itself can cause transient page traffic. recommended: ensure routing spreads sessions, or reserve GPUs for hot workloads.

[03:56] Ben: we observed periodic spikes every ~30 minutes correlated with a background batch job. could that be eviction churn?

[04:03] Priya: sounds like it. background jobs that allocate large buffers or run compile/cache sweeps can pressure memory and trigger mass evictions. look for simultaneous increase in cache.evictions and pages_out in the timeline.

[04:15] Jordan: let's walk through a troubleshooting checklist. step 1: capture a timeline of cache.hit_rate, evictions, pages_out, gpu.memory.used, and memcopy durations. step 2: check request patterns for long-only sessions that pin but are idle. step 3: test cache pinning or move system prompts to pinned tier. step 4: run a benchmark with prefix reuse to measure warm vs cold latency.

[04:41] Carlos: is there an automated warmup? we have many short-lived sessions but they reuse common prefixes.

[04:49] Priya: we support proactive warming policies. you can pre-seed the cache by replaying prefixes at low priority or using an explicit warm API. for high reuse prefixes we can keep a cold/warm threshold - warm entries live in GPU RAM and cold entries stored compressed in host RAM. warmup reduces the first-call latency.

[05:06] Aisha: how do we measure warming success?

[05:10] Priya: measure prefix_hit_rate and time_to_first_token for warm vs cold states. warmup increases prefix_hit_rate close to 1.0 and reduces first-token latency significantly. we also track cache_residency_seconds per prefix.

[05:27] Ben: you mentioned eviction policies - do you support LFU or hybrid LRU/LFU?

[05:32] Priya: runtime supports LRU by default, but there's a hybrid LRU-LFU mode and TTL thresholds. LFU is useful when a small set of prefixes is frequently reused but LRU works well for temporal locality. hybrid can be tuned per workload.

[05:47] Carlos: what about long-context windows, say 8k-32k? how does the KV cache scale?

[05:54] Priya: KV size grows linearly with sequence length times layers and hidden dimension. going from 4k to 32k is 8x KV size. we rely on quantization, sharding, and eviction tiers. for true long context we recommend architectures that crop or summarize older context, or use chunked attention variants. runtime can also stream older KV to NVMe and keep only recent tokens warm.

[06:20] Jordan: practical tradeoffs - for worst-case latency SLOs you want to avoid paging entirely: ensure enough reserved GPU RAM, pin hot prefixes, and use quantized KV. if you accept occasional higher tail, the paging to NVMe is a reasonable fallback.

[06:36] Aisha: regarding logs/diagnostics, can you show the exact log keys we should grep?

[06:40] Priya: sure. logs include keys like cache.hit_rate.route, cache.evictions.total, cache.pageouts.ns, cache.pageins.ns, kv_cache.residency_seconds, kv_cache.pin_actions, runtime.mempressure.events. also our debug agent can dump per-session KV sizes. we'll share the doc.

[06:58] Carlos: any gotchas with batching? we saw that higher batching reduces throughput variance but sometimes increases memory footprint and unexpectedly evicts caches.

[07:07] Priya: batching increases simultaneous token work and may increase transient KV allocations if multiple sessions advance together. that can increase peak memory. smart batching policies that cap batch depth and do prefix-aware batching help. also batching with pinned prefixes should be prioritized to avoid eviction.

[07:26] Ben: do kernel optimizations or quantization change KV layout so cached entries are incompatible after a model update?

[07:33] Priya: yes. model version or execution path changes can invalidate cached KV entries. we version cache keys with model_id+variant+execution_path hash. on rollout you might see cache thrash; we recommend staged rollouts and warm rehydration after model changes.

[07:51] Jordan: quick interjection, we have a sample rehydration script we can run as part of rollout to pre-seed caches with representative prefixes.

[07:58] Aisha: one more concern - we run private VPC with restricted egress. if NVMe fallback uses ephemeral local SSD, is any network egress required?

[08:06] Priya: no, NVMe fallback is local to node. for Private deployments, everything stays in your VPC and NVMe is local. if you rely on a central cache service, that may require intra-cluster network traffic but not external egress.

[08:18] Carlos: ok let's go through a reproducible failure we saw last week. we had 95th latency jump from 180ms to 1.4s for certain sessions after a nightly batch. we have traces showing memcopy spikes and pageins. thoughts?

[08:31] Priya: that aligns with mass eviction due to memory pressure. steps: check cache.evictions timeline, identify which sessions triggered big allocations, check if pinned entries were forced out, and review batching schedule for overlap with nightly jobs. mitigation: move nightly job to lower priority, reserve GPUs, or increase KV capacity via quantization or extra nodes.

[08:54] Ben: is there a recommended eviction threshold config?

[08:57] Priya: default triggers at 85% GPU mem use with progressive eviction. you can tighten to 75% to avoid sudden paging; tradeoff is lower utilization. we can help tune for your SLOs.

[09:09] Carlos: what about instrumentation for customer-visible errors when cache pages fail? we saw stalled sessions but no clear error code.

[09:17] Priya: runtime emits a specific runtime.code CACHE_PAGE_TIMEOUT or CACHE_FAULT with context. we also surface per-request annotations, like cache_warm=true/false, pagein_ms, and evicted_prefixes list. if you enable verbose tracing we can attach trace ids.

[09:33] Jordan: alright we're about halfway through. open Qs?

[09:36] Aisha: does quantization affect page-in bandwidth? smaller tensors mean less PCIe transfer so yes. any recommended quant config?

[09:44] Priya: start with 8-bit quant on KV, test quality. if acceptable, move to 4-bit with per-layer scale. we provide conversion tools and evaluation harness. quant reduces both memory usage and transfer time on page-in.

[09:57] Carlos: any sample numbers? like 8k context latency hot vs cold?

[10:02] Priya: approximate numbers on modern A100-class nodes: warmed 8k prefix first token 45-80ms, cold with page-in to host RAM 200-400ms, page-in to NVMe 600ms-1.2s depending PCIe. quantized KV can cut page-in bandwidth by 2-4x so cold path improves proportionally. these are rough, we'll run your exact benchmark.

[10:27] Ben: if we enable pinned prefixes plus warmup, how much extra RAM headroom should we reserve?

[10:32] Priya: depends on prefix sizes. measure per-prefix KV size in bytes, multiply by expected concurrent pinned sessions, add safety buffer 20-30%. example: 2k token prefix for 32-layer model might be X MB per session. we'll provide a sizing calculator.

[10:47] Carlos: last technical question - how do you handle partial eviction in the middle of generation?

[10:54] Priya: runtime avoids evicting KV for sessions currently generating; evictions target idle sessions and least-recently-used prefixes. if memory pressure is severe we may checkpoint and page parts of KV for idle sessions only. partial eviction for an active session is a last resort and is guarded by heuristics; if it happens you will see increased per-token latency for that session.

[11:14] Jordan: time for a short recap and concrete next steps. we will share docs: KV design doc, pinning config, warmup API, log keys, and the sample rehydration script. Acme will share traces and prompt prefixes. we'll schedule a benchmark run targeted at 8k context with prefix reuse.

[11:31] Carlos: that sounds good. can Priya include the recommended config snippets for LRU vs hybrid?

[11:36] Priya: yes will include examples and suggested thresholds.

[11:40] Aisha: thanks everyone.

[11:42] Jordan: thanks team. we'll follow up in email with links: the KV design doc, the benchmark spreadsheet, and the warmup API spec. links: https://redwood.example.com/docs/kv-cache-design (doc), https://redwood.example.com/sheets/kv-benchmarks (benchmark sheet).

End of meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional transcription artifacts present - K V sometimes transcribed as K V, memcopy sometimes mem copy, and certain acronyms may be mis-capitalized.
